title: When the earth shakes on fragile foundations: the Venezuelan earthquakes and two decades of public health system erosion

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《When the earth shakes on fragile foundations: the Venezuelan earthquakes and two decades of public health system erosion》：研究问题的原文依据。

【Introduction · p0010】On June 24, 2026, two exceptionally strong earthquakes (Mw 7.2 and Mw 7.5) struck the north–central coast of Venezuela just seconds apart, causing a significant devastation in seven states.1 This near-simultaneous sequence constitutes one of the most catastrophic seismic events in the country’s recent history. Two epicenters were identified, one in between Yaracuy and Carabobo states, and the second off the coast of La Guaira state, with the greatest destruction concentrated in the cities of Catia La Mar and Caraballeda, both in La Guaira. Within hours, the U.S. Geological Survey’s Global Earthquake Rapid Assessment for Response (PAGER) system estimated a 42% probability of between 10,000 and 100,000 fatalities, highlighting the anticipated severity of the disaster.1 At the time of the events, emergency services were overwhelmed by the scale of the demand, as well as disruptions in telecommunications, water, electricity, and transportation systems, which triggered an immediate international humanitarian response.2 As of August 10, 2026, the latest official reports document 6301 deaths, approximately 73,356 hospitalizations and 6462 rescued people.3 The number of victims could rise and get close to the lower end of the projection made by PAGER, given that debris removal efforts are still ongoing, having only reached 23.3% of the projected total.3 By August 12, 2026, according to the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO),4 28 transitional camps had been established in La Guaira and Miranda states, and the Capital District, sheltering approximately 12,752 displaced people. Meanwhile, according to the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA),3 by August 14, 2026, more than 304,000 people affected by the earthquakes across the seven directly affected states had accessed essential services and humanitarian assistance (Fig. 1).

【Introduction · p0015】The devastation and humanitarian consequences of the ongoing Venezuelan earthquakes cannot be explained solely by their geophysical magnitude. Rather, they are the culmination of more than two decades of institutional deterioration, during which health systems, public infrastructure, and scientific capacity eroded, leaving the country extremely vulnerable to major emergencies. While direct comparisons between events in different countries are complex, the remarkably lower toll of the similar Mw 7.4 earthquake that affected neighboring Colombia less than two months later, on August 10, 2026 (304 documented deaths, 4548 injuries, 426 missing persons, and 292,043 people affected)5,6 highlights Venezuela’s manifest institutional vulnerability.

sections.title: 研究方法
sections.text:
《When the earth shakes on fragile foundations: the Venezuelan earthquakes and two decades of public health system erosion》：方法与研究设计的原文依据。

【A health system with limited disaster preparedness · p0030】At the time of the earthquakes, the states, Capital District, La Guaira and Miranda had only 97 public health centers of different categories in operation (25 tertiary, 34 secondaries, 38 primary).9 However, PAHO’s rapid assessments of eight representative main public hospitals found structural damage in three and urgent needs for external support in all, with only 1220 beds available in total for an area with a combined population of approximately 6 million people.9 The reduced capacity accentuated the need for emergency supplies, trauma care, facility assessments, and operational coordination. The initial response required mobilization of national and international resources, including patient transfers to private hospitals and deployment of eleven international field hospitals.2 Emergency Medical Teams (EMTs) were coordinated on the field; but by August 12, 2026, only nine remained active across La Guaira, Caracas, and Miranda, while thirteen had demobilized.4 Seven weeks later, national and international operations continue to sustain emergency care while transitioning toward early recovery.

【Preserving essential health services and the scale of recovery beyond immediate damage · p0085】This response draws attention to a dimension of disaster medicine that is frequently overlooked: continuity of care for chronic infectious diseases matters as much as the management of acute trauma. If antiretroviral therapy, tuberculosis treatment or diagnostic services are interrupted, the consequences for the individual patient are immediate, and the risks of transmission, treatment failure and drug resistance also rise.

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:
《When the earth shakes on fragile foundations: the Venezuelan earthquakes and two decades of public health system erosion》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【Conclusion · p0105】The earthquakes of June 2026 in Venezuela exposed the fragility of a health system eroded by institutional decay, chronic underinvestment, and a loss of capacity. These events did not create new vulnerabilities but rather revealed and exacerbated existing ones. Over the subsequent 6–24 months, PAHO, the UNDP, national institutions, and international partners must leverage the recovery period to rebuild essential systems. Priority must be given to rehabilitating damaged facilities and ensuring continuity of care while restoring hospital services, basic utilities, supply chains, laboratories, and epidemiologic surveillance systems. Progress should be assessed at the 6-, 12-, and 24-month marks using indicators such as hospital functionality, continuity of treatment and vaccination, diagnostic reliability, and the operational status of emergency plans, including seismic monitoring.

【Conclusion · p0110】Long-term recovery requires rebuilding the foundations of public health and strengthening governance to ensure transparency and equity. This involves having functional facilities, effective supply chains, robust surveillance systems, laboratory capacity, sufficient health personnel, and institutions capable of delivering effective care. While natural phenomena cannot be prevented, their impact can be mitigated. Critically, Venezuela’s experience demonstrates that pre-existing institutional weaknesses are often as damaging as the natural disaster that leaves them in evidence.

sections.title: 图表阅读
sections.text:
《When the earth shakes on fragile foundations: the Venezuelan earthquakes and two decades of public health system erosion》：图表的原始标题与说明。

【Fig. 1 · fig1】Fig. 1 Map of Venezuela showing states affected by the two earthquakes, shaded by impact level. Inset (upper right) depicts Venezuela within South America. Map generated with QGIS software (https://www.qgis.org/es/site/).

【Fig. 2 · fig2】Fig. 2 Heatmap showing vaccine coverage (%) in Venezuela from 2016 to 2025 for seven essential vaccines: BCG (tuberculosis), DTP1 and DTP3 (diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis, first and third doses, respectively), IPV1 (polio, first dose), MCV1 and MCV2 (measles, first and second doses, respectively), and YFV (yellow fever). Coverage levels are color-coded to highlight declines and partial recoveries across the decade. Source: WHO/UNICEF estimates of national immunization coverage (https://worldhealthorg.shinyapps.io/wuenic-trends/).
